questions.question: A girl throws a small stone into a lake. Waves spread out from where the stone hits the water and travel to the bank of the lake. She notices that ten waves reach the side of the pond in a time of 5.0 s. What is the frequency of the waves?
questions.explanation: Frequency is defined as the number of complete waves passing a point per second. Using f = N / t = 10 / 5.0 s = 2.0 Hz.

questions.question: Water waves can be used to show reflection, refraction, and diffraction. For each of these, which row shows whether or not the speed of the water waves changes?

options.text: Reflection: No / Refraction: Yes / Diffraction: No

questions.optionsRaw: c) Reflection: No / Refraction: Yes / Diffraction: No
questions.correctAnswer: c) Reflection: No / Refraction: Yes / Diffraction: No
questions.explanation: During reflection and diffraction, the wave remains in the same medium, so its speed remains constant. In refraction, the wave moves from one medium/depth to another, which changes its speed.

questions.question: The diagrams show water waves that move more slowly after passing into shallow water. Which diagram shows what happens to the waves?
questions.explanation: When water waves pass into shallow water, their speed and wavelength decrease, causing wavefronts to get closer together and bend toward the normal.

questions.question: The diagram shows a water wave approaching a barrier with a gap. The wave reaches point P. What is the name of the effect that causes the wave to reach point P?
questions.explanation: Diffraction is the spreading of waves as they pass through an aperture or around an obstacle into the shadow region.

questions.question: Water waves pass from deep into the shallow region then refracted. The characteristic of wave which will remain constant is:
questions.explanation: The frequency of a wave is determined solely by the source generating the wave and remains unchanged during refraction.

questions.question: Which is not a characteristic of wave?
questions.explanation: Waves transfer energy and momentum without transporting mass. Wavelength, amplitude, period, and velocity are wave characteristics.

questions.question: When an oscillating object is in simple harmonic motion, its maximum speed occurs when the object is at its:
questions.explanation: At the equilibrium point, all potential energy is converted into kinetic energy, so speed is maximum.

questions.question: In an oscillating pendulum, the bob accelerates from its extreme position due to:
questions.explanation: The restoring component of gravity (mg sin θ) pulls the bob back toward the central rest position.

questions.question: In the ball and bowl system, the mean position is at:
questions.explanation: At the center of the bowl, net force acting on the ball is zero (normal reaction balances weight).

questions.question: Oscillations are damped due to the presence of:
questions.explanation: Damping occurs when resistive/frictional forces dissipate mechanical energy into thermal energy.

questions.question: How spherical wavefronts are produced in the ripple tank?
questions.answer: Spherical wavefronts are produced by using a point dipper (a small spherical ball attached to the vibrator) that touches the water surface at a single point.
questions.explanation: As the point dipper oscillates vertically, it creates circular/spherical ripples that expand uniformly outward in all directions.

questions.question: What is the difference between displacement and amplitude of the wave?
questions.answer: Displacement (x) is the distance of a vibrating particle from its equilibrium position at any given instant. Amplitude (A) is the maximum displacement of a particle from its equilibrium position.
questions.explanation: Displacement varies continuously from zero to maximum, whereas amplitude is a fixed constant representing peak displacement.

questions.question: Derive the relation between wave speed and frequency.
questions.answer: v = f λ
questions.explanation: Speed is distance divided by time (v = S / t). For one full wave cycle, distance S = λ (wavelength) and time t = T (period). Thus v = λ / T. Since frequency f = 1 / T, substituting gives v = f λ.

questions.question: Define the term transverse wave.
questions.answer: A transverse wave is a wave in which the particles of the medium vibrate perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation.
questions.explanation: Examples include water waves, light waves, and waves on a plucked string.

questions.question: Define the term longitudinal wave.
questions.answer: A longitudinal wave is a wave in which the particles of the medium vibrate parallel to the direction of wave propagation.
questions.explanation: It consists of compressions (high density) and rarefactions (low density). Examples include sound waves and slinky compression waves.

questions.question: a) Write a short note on the mechanical wave. b) How can you say that mechanical waves are also material waves?
questions.answer: a) Mechanical waves require a physical material medium (solid, liquid, or gas) to travel and transmit energy. b) They are called material waves because energy transfer depends entirely on elastic collisions between material particles of the medium.
questions.explanation: They cannot propagate through a vacuum (e.g. sound waves, water waves).

questions.question: Waves are the means of energy transfer without matter. Justify this statement with the help of everyday life examples.
questions.answer: When a stone is dropped into a pond, water ripples move outward and cause a distant floating leaf to bob up and down at its position without traveling along with the wave to the shore.
questions.explanation: This proves that energy is transferred across distances while the medium particles only oscillate locally about their mean position.

questions.question: a) Define amplitude, period, frequency, and wavelength. b) Derive v = f λ.
questions.answer: a) Amplitude: Maximum displacement from equilibrium position. Period (T): Time taken for one complete oscillation. Frequency (f): Number of complete cycles per second. Wavelength (λ): Distance between two consecutive crests/compressions. b) Derived from v = S/t = λ/T = f λ.
questions.explanation: Key fundamental wave relationships.

questions.question: a) What is a ripple tank, and explain its working? b) Define wavefront.
questions.answer: a) A ripple tank is a shallow glass tray filled with water, illuminated from above, used to demonstrate wave reflection, refraction, and diffraction. Motorized dippers generate periodic water waves whose crests/troughs appear as light/dark bands on a screen underneath. b) A wavefront is a surface or line joining all points vibrating in the same phase.
questions.explanation: Essential laboratory tool for wave optics and dynamics.

questions.question: Reference an experiment to explain the refraction of waves concerning the ripple tank.
questions.answer: Place a flat glass plate in part of the ripple tank to decrease water depth. When water waves pass from deep water to shallow water at an angle, their speed and wavelength decrease, causing the wavefronts to bend toward the normal line.
questions.explanation: Demonstrates refraction due to medium density/depth change.

questions.question: What is the phenomenon of diffraction?
questions.answer: Diffraction is the bending or spreading of wave wavefronts around the corners of obstacles or through narrow gaps/apertures into the shadow region.
questions.explanation: Diffraction is most pronounced when the gap size is comparable to the wavelength.

questions.question: a) What is simple harmonic motion (SHM)? b) What are the necessary conditions for a body to execute SHM?
questions.answer: a) SHM is periodic motion where acceleration is directly proportional to displacement from the mean position and directed toward the mean position (a ∝ -x). b) Conditions: 1. Restoring force proportional to displacement (F = -kx). 2. System possesses inertia and elasticity. 3. Minimal friction/damping.
questions.explanation: Governs linear restoring systems.

questions.question: a) Explain SHM in a simple pendulum. b) Effect on period if: i) length increases, ii) mass increases.
questions.answer: a) A pendulum bob displaced by angle θ experiences a restoring gravitational force component (mg sin θ) pulling it toward the mean position. b) i) Increasing length L increases time period T (since T ∝ √L). ii) Mass has no effect on period T.
questions.explanation: Formula: T = 2π √(L/g).

questions.question: a) Explain SHM in the ball and bowl system. b) Why is ball speed maximum at equilibrium position?
questions.answer: a) When a ball is released from an elevated rim point A in a smooth bowl, gravity pulls it toward the central mean position O. Momentum carries it to opposite point B, oscillating in SHM. b) At equilibrium, all potential energy is converted into kinetic energy (PE=0, KE=max).
questions.explanation: Demonstrates gravitational restoring motion.

questions.question: a) What are damped oscillations? b) How does damping reduce amplitude? c) Why does a swing's amplitude decrease with time?
questions.answer: a) Damped oscillations are vibrations whose amplitude decreases progressively over time due to resistive forces. b) Friction and air resistance perform negative work, dissipating energy into heat. c) Air drag and hinge friction drain energy from the swing until it stops.
questions.explanation: Energy dissipation in real physical systems.

questions.question: Numerical 1: Wavelength of broadcasted radio wave
questions.answer:
Given Data:
Frequency f = 1300 kHz = 1.3 × 10^6 HzWave speed v = 3 × 10^8 m/s

Formula: λ = v / f

Calculation: λ = (3 × 10^8) / (1.3 × 10^6) = 230.77 m

Result: Wavelength λ = 230.77 m
questions.explanation: Calculated using the fundamental wave equation.

questions.question: Numerical 2: Speed of water waves in pond
questions.answer:
Given Data:
Wavelength λ = 1.6 mFrequency f = 0.80 Hz

Formula: v = f λ

Calculation: v = 0.80 × 1.6 = 1.28 m/s

Result: Wave speed v = 1.28 m/s
questions.explanation: Direct application of wave speed relation.

questions.question: Numerical 3: Rope wave parameters
questions.answer:
Given Data:
Number of waves N = 50Time t = 10 sWavelength λ = 8 cm = 0.08 m

Formula: f = N / t, T = 1 / f, v = f λ

Calculation: f = 50 / 10 = 5 HzT = 1 / 5 = 0.2 sv = 5 × 0.08 = 0.4 m/s

Result: Frequency = 5 Hz, Period = 0.2 s, Speed = 0.4 m/s (Transverse Wave)
questions.explanation: Particles vibrate up and down perpendicular to wave travel, so it is a transverse wave.

questions.question: Numerical 4: Slinky compression distance
questions.answer:
Given Data:
Speed v = 40 cm/s = 0.40 m/sFrequency f = 20 Hz

Formula: λ = v / f

Calculation: λ = 0.40 / 20 = 0.02 m = 2 cm

Result: Minimum separation between consecutive compressions λ = 0.02 m (2 cm)
questions.explanation: Distance between consecutive compressions equals one wavelength.

questions.question: Numerical 5: Slinky wave oscillation parameters
questions.answer:
Given Data:
Time for one cycle T = 0.40 sWavelength λ = 0.60 m

Formula: f = 1 / T, v = f λ

Calculation: a) Period T = 0.40 s, Frequency f = 1 / 0.40 = 2.5 Hzb) Speed v = 2.5 × 0.60 = 1.5 m/s

Result: Period = 0.40 s, Frequency = 2.5 Hz, Wave speed = 1.5 m/s
questions.explanation: Complete calculation from period to frequency and speed.

questions.question: Numerical 6: Spring compression wave parameters
questions.answer:
Given Data:
Compressions N = 80Time t = 20 sSeparation λ = 8 cm = 0.08 m

Formula: f = N / t, T = 1 / f, v = f λ

Calculation: f = 80 / 20 = 4 HzT = 1 / 4 = 0.25 sv = 4 × 0.08 = 0.32 m/s

Result: Frequency = 4 Hz, Period = 0.25 s, Speed = 0.32 m/s
questions.explanation: Standard longitudinal compression wave analysis.

questions.question: Numerical 7: Swimming pool round-trip reflection
questions.answer:
Given Data:
Speed v = 0.90 m/sRound trip time t = 30.0 s

Formula: Total distance S = v × t, Pool length d = S / 2, Frequency f = 1 / t

Calculation: Total distance S = 0.90 × 30.0 = 27 mPool length d = 27 / 2 = 13.5 mCycle frequency = 1 / 30.0 = 0.033 Hz

Result: Pool length = 13.5 m, Total wave travel = 27 m, Frequency = 0.033 Hz
questions.explanation: The wave travels across the pool and back, so pool distance is half the total distance.

questions.question: Numerical 8: Simple oscillating pendulum
questions.answer:
Given Data:
Length L = 80.0 cm = 0.80 mGravitational acceleration g = 9.8 m/s²

Formula: T = 2π √(L/g), f = 1 / T

Calculation: a) T = 2 × 3.1416 × √(0.80 / 9.8) = 6.2832 × 0.2857 = 1.794 sb) f = 1 / 1.794 = 0.557 Hz

Result: Period T = 1.794 s, Frequency f = 0.557 Hz
questions.explanation: Period depends only on length L and gravitational acceleration g.

questions.question: Sound is a form of:
questions.explanation: Sound requires a material medium to propagate and transfers mechanical energy through particle vibrations.

questions.question: Audible frequencies range that a normal human ear can detect is:
questions.explanation: The human audible frequency spectrum spans from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz).

questions.question: The approximate value of the speed of sound in air at 0°C temperature is:
questions.explanation: At standard temperature and pressure (0°C), the speed of sound in dry air is 331 m/s.

questions.question: Sound travels faster in solids as compared to gases because of:
questions.optionsRaw: c) Solid molecules are packed tightly.
questions.correctAnswer: c) Solid molecules are packed tightly.
questions.explanation: Tight molecular packing in solids results in higher elasticity and quicker particle-to-particle energy transmission.

questions.question: The two factors that affect the speed of sound in air are:

options.text: Temperature and humidity of the air

questions.optionsRaw: d) Temperature and humidity of the air
questions.correctAnswer: d) Temperature and humidity of the air
questions.explanation: Increasing air temperature and humidity both reduce density, thereby increasing sound speed.

questions.question: The separation between two consecutive compressions of the sound wave is called:
questions.explanation: Wavelength in a longitudinal wave is the distance between consecutive compressions or rarefactions.

questions.question: The order of speed of the sound in different mediums from faster to slowest is:
questions.explanation: Sound travels fastest in dense solids (e.g. steel ~5960 m/s), slower in liquids (~1498 m/s in water), slowest in gases (~340 m/s in air).

questions.question: Ultrasound has several uses in medicine and industry. Which one has use of ultrasound?
questions.explanation: High-frequency ultrasound waves (2-18 MHz) are non-invasive and safe for fetal imaging.

questions.question: The cause of the echo is:
questions.explanation: An echo is caused by the reflection of sound waves off a hard surface back to the listener.

questions.question: Which type of wave cannot travel through a vacuum?
questions.explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave requiring physical particle vibrations and cannot propagate in a vacuum.

questions.question: Product of resistance and capacitance equal to?
questions.answer: Time (T). Unit is Seconds (s).
questions.explanation: Dimensionally: R = V / I = J / (C · A), C = Q / V = C / V. R · C = (V / I) · (Q / V) = Q / I = (A · s) / A = Seconds.

questions.question: a) How is sound produced? b) Describe compressions and rarefactions with a diagram.
questions.answer: a) Sound is produced by vibrating bodies that disturb adjacent air particles. b) Compressions are high-pressure, high-density regions where particles are pushed together. Rarefactions are low-pressure, low-density regions where particles spread apart.
questions.explanation: Vibrating tuning forks or speaker cones displace air to form longitudinal pressure waves.

questions.question: a) Why are sound waves referred to as mechanical waves? b) Cite an experiment proving sound requires a medium.
questions.answer: a) Sound waves require a physical material medium (solid, liquid, or gas) to transmit vibrations. b) Bell Jar Experiment: Place an electric bell inside an airtight glass jar connected to a vacuum pump. As air is evacuated, the ringing sound fades until it becomes silent, proving sound cannot travel in a vacuum.
questions.explanation: Classic physics demonstration of mechanical wave medium requirement.

questions.question: a) Distinguish between musical sound and noise. b) How is noise harmful to humans?
questions.answer: a) Musical sound consists of regular, periodic, pleasing vibrations. Noise consists of irregular, non-periodic, unpleasant vibrations. b) Prolonged noise exposure causes stress, hearing loss, hypertension, and sleep disruption.
questions.explanation: Acoustic quality and noise pollution impacts.

questions.question: a) Define quality or timbre of sound. b) Can two waves from different instruments combine into one wave?
questions.answer: a) Quality or timbre is the characteristic of sound that enables us to distinguish between two notes of the same pitch and loudness produced by different instruments due to different waveforms/overtones. b) Yes, superposing waves construct a resultant complex wave.
questions.explanation: Overtones determine sound texture.

questions.question: a) Why is sound speed greater in solids than liquids/gases? b) Effect of temperature and humidity on sound speed in air.
questions.answer: a) Solids have much higher elastic moduli (stiffness) and tightly packed molecules, transmitting disturbance forces rapidly. b) i) Increasing temperature increases air particle kinetic energy, raising sound speed (~0.6 m/s per °C). ii) Increasing humidity replaces heavier N2/O2 molecules with lighter H2O molecules, reducing air density and increasing sound speed.
questions.explanation: Dependence of acoustic velocity on medium elasticity and density.

questions.question: a) Define echo. b) Explain working and applications of SONAR. c) Detection of defects in metal blocks using ultrasound.
questions.answer: a) An echo is the repetition of sound caused by the reflection of sound waves from a distant hard barrier. b) SONAR (Sound Navigation and Ranging) transmits ultrasonic pulses downward into water and measures the return echo time to determine seabed depth or underwater objects (d = v · t / 2). c) Ultrasonic waves sent through metal blocks pass through clean metal but reflect back early from internal cracks/flaws.
questions.explanation: Acoustic reflection diagnostic applications.

questions.question: a) Define Infrasonic, Audible range, Ultrasound. b) How is ultrasound used for cleaning? c) Two medical imaging uses of ultrasound.
questions.answer: a) Infrasonic: Sound below 20 Hz. Audible range: 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Ultrasound: Sound above 20,000 Hz (20 kHz). b) High-frequency ultrasonic vibrations in cleaning solutions dislodge dirt from intricate instrument parts. c) i) Pre-natal fetal monitoring. ii) Echocardiography for heart imaging.
questions.explanation: Frequency classification and medical/industrial ultrasound.

questions.question: Numerical 1: Speed of sound in air at 50°C
questions.answer:
Given Data:
Speed at 0°C v0 = 331 m/sTemperature T = 50°C

Formula: vt = 331 + 0.6 × T

Calculation: vt = 331 + 0.6 × 50 = 331 + 30 = 361.0 m/s

Result: Speed of sound at 50°C = 361.0 m/s
questions.explanation: Temperature correction formula for acoustic speed in air.

questions.question: Numerical 2: Wavelengths corresponding to human audible frequency range
questions.answer:
Given Data:
f1 = 20 Hz, f2 = 20 kHz = 20,000 HzSound speed v = 340 m/s

Formula: λ = v / f

Calculation: λ1 = 340 / 20 = 17.0 mλ2 = 340 / 20,000 = 0.017 m (1.7 cm)

Result: Audible wavelength range = 17.0 m to 0.017 m (17.2 m / 0.172 m under specific STB constant sets)
questions.explanation: Higher frequency corresponds to shorter wavelength.

questions.question: Numerical 3: Submarine depth measurement using ultrasonic pulse
questions.answer:
Given Data:
Echo time t = 40 ms = 0.040 sSound speed in seawater v = 1480 m/s

Formula: d = (v × t) / 2

Calculation: d = (1480 × 0.040) / 2 = 59.2 / 2 = 29.6 m ≈ 30 m

Result: Submarine depth = 29.6 m (rounded to 30 m)
questions.explanation: Echo travels down to sea-bed and back, so single-way depth is half the total distance.

questions.question: Numerical 4: Bat echolocation prey detection
questions.answer:
Given Data:
Wavelength λ = 0.0080 m, Speed in air v = 340 m/s, Return echo time t = 0.10 s

Formula: i) f = v / λii) Total distance = v × tiii) Prey distance d = (v × t) / 2

Calculation: i) f = 340 / 0.0080 = 42,500 Hz = 42.5 kHzii) Total pulse distance = 340 × 0.10 = 34 miii) Prey distance = 34 / 2 = 17 m

Result: i) Frequency = 42.5 kHzii) Total pulse distance = 34 miii) Distance to prey = 17 m
questions.explanation: Bat echolocation uses ultrasonic reflection to pinpoint prey distance.

questions.question: The waves that have maximum penetrating power to treat tumors are:
questions.explanation: Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength, highest frequency, and highest energy in the EM spectrum.

questions.question: The electromagnetic rays used in radiotherapy to destroy cancer cells are:
questions.explanation: Targeted X-rays and Gamma rays destroy cancerous tumor DNA.

questions.question: The velocity of light in a diamond is (refractive index of diamond = 2.5):
The group containing only electromagnetic waves is:
questions.optionsRaw: a) Light waves, Radio waves, Microwaves
questions.correctAnswer: a) Light waves, Radio waves, Microwaves
questions.explanation: Sound waves are mechanical waves, while light, radio, and microwaves are all non-mechanical EM waves.

questions.question: The list that shows electromagnetic waves in order of an increasing wavelength is:
questions.explanation: EM order from shortest to longest wavelength: Gamma-rays < X-rays < Ultraviolet < Visible < Infrared < Microwaves < Radio waves.

questions.question: The type of electromagnetic wave used in security scanners at night is:
questions.explanation: Infrared sensors detect thermal heat radiation emitted by warm objects in pitch darkness.

questions.question: A narrow beam of white light passes from air into glass and is refracted. The wave characteristic remaining unchanged is:
questions.explanation: Frequency is determined by the source and never changes during refraction.

questions.question: The type of waves used in television remote controllers:
questions.explanation: TV remotes transmit coded pulsed infrared light signals to receivers.

questions.question: The color that is least deviated by a prism:
questions.explanation: Red light has the longest visible wavelength and lowest refractive index in glass, so it deviates least.

questions.question: The optical phenomenon in which the splitting of white light into seven distinct colors occurs is called:
questions.explanation: Dispersion is the separation of composite white light into constituent spectrum colors due to wavelength-dependent refraction.

questions.question: a) Define dispersion of light. b) Describe dispersion when white light passes through a glass prism.
questions.answer: a) Dispersion is the splitting of composite white light into its constituent spectral colors when passing through a refracting medium. b) When white light enters a glass prism, each constituent wavelength refracts at a slightly different angle because glass refractive index varies with wavelength. Red (longest λ) bends least, while Violet (shortest λ) bends most, producing a VIBGYOR spectrum.
questions.explanation: Prism refracts colors according to wavelength.

questions.question: a) Explain how a rainbow is produced on a rainy day. b) How are spectrum colors related to frequency/wavelength?
questions.answer: a) Millions of airborne raindrops act as tiny glass prisms. Sunlight entering a raindrop refracts, internally reflects off the back wall, and refracts again upon exiting, dispersing light into a rainbow arc. b) Violet has the highest frequency and shortest wavelength (~400 nm); Red has the lowest frequency and longest wavelength (~700 nm).
questions.explanation: Atmospheric dispersion and internal reflection.

questions.question: a) What are electromagnetic waves? b) List main EM components in decreasing order of wavelength. c) Do UV rays travel faster than radio waves in a vacuum?
questions.answer: a) EM waves are transverse non-mechanical waves consisting of oscillating electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to each other and to propagation direction. b) Decreasing wavelength: Radio waves > Microwaves > Infrared > Visible Light > Ultraviolet > X-rays > Gamma rays. c) No, all EM waves travel at the exact same speed in a vacuum (c = 3 × 10^8 m/s).
questions.explanation: Maxwellian electromagnetic wave principles.

questions.question: Compare properties of UV rays and radio signals: a) Faster speed in vacuum? b) Greater frequency? c) Greater wavelength?
questions.answer: a) Both have equal speed in a vacuum (c = 3 × 10^8 m/s). b) Ultraviolet rays have a much greater frequency than radio waves. c) Radio waves have a much greater wavelength than UV rays.
questions.explanation: Speed is constant c = f λ.

questions.question: a) What are main sources of radio waves? b) Main advantage of radio waves in communication?
questions.answer: a) Radio transmitters (oscillating LC circuits/antennas), astronomical objects (stars, pulsars). b) Long wavelength allows radio waves to diffract around buildings, pass through atmospheric obstacles, and travel vast distances.
questions.explanation: Telecommunication foundations.

questions.question: Why are microwaves preferred in satellite communication?
questions.answer: Microwaves (high frequency, short wavelength) can pass straight through the Earth's ionosphere without reflection or significant absorption, establishing direct line-of-sight links with orbiting satellites.
questions.explanation: Ionospheric transmission window.

questions.question: a) Radiation used in TV remote controllers? b) How do molecules emit infrared? c) How do intruder alarms visualize thermal images?
questions.answer: a) Infrared radiation. b) Thermal vibrations and rotations of charged molecular bonds emit infrared photons. c) Passive Infrared (PIR) sensors detect changes in thermal IR patterns emitted by moving human body heat against cool surroundings.
questions.explanation: Infrared technology applications.

questions.question: a) Principle of optical fibers? b) Daily life applications in telecommunications and medical industry.
questions.answer: a) Total Internal Reflection (TIR) inside a high-refractive-index core surrounded by lower-index cladding. b) i) Telecommunications: High-speed fiber optic internet transmitting data pulses at light speed over long distances without electrical loss. ii) Medical: Endoscopes for non-surgical internal organ imaging.
questions.explanation: Fiber optics and total internal reflection.

questions.question: a) Sunlight exposure and skin damage. b) Why UV rays are used under medical supervision in sunbeds.
questions.answer: a) Sunlight contains UV-A and UV-B radiation that can damage cellular DNA and cause sunburn or skin cancer. Controlled short exposure stimulates Vitamin D synthesis. b) Controlled UV dosages treat skin disorders like psoriasis while avoiding carcinogenic tissue damage.
questions.explanation: Biological impacts of ultraviolet radiation.

questions.question: a) Explain fluorescence. b) Describe sterilization using UV light.
questions.answer: a) Fluorescence is the absorption of higher-frequency UV radiation by a material, which re-emits visible light photons almost instantaneously. b) Short-wavelength UV-C radiation destroys bacterial and viral DNA/RNA, sterilizing medical instruments and water.
questions.explanation: Photonic absorption and sterilization.

questions.question: X-rays are used to detect cracks in metals. Explain how.
questions.answer: High-energy X-rays penetrate dense metal components and strike a photographic film or digital detector behind them. Cracks or internal voids allow more X-rays through, creating dark lines on the radiograph.
questions.explanation: Industrial radiography inspection.

questions.question: a) Origin of gamma rays? b) Radiosurgery cancer treatment. c) Hospital medical imaging applications.
questions.answer: a) Gamma rays originate from de-excitation transitions within unstable radioactive atomic nuclei. b) Gamma Knife radiosurgery focuses multiple weak gamma beams from different angles onto a deep brain tumor to destroy cancer cells without harming healthy tissue. c) PET scans and SPECT imaging use gamma-emitting tracers for diagnostic body scans.
questions.explanation: Nuclear medical radiation applications.

questions.question: Numerical 1: Frequency of 15.0 μm infrared radiation
questions.answer:
Given Data:
Wavelength λ = 15.0 μm = 15.0 × 10^-6 mLight speed c = 3 × 10^8 m/s

Formula: f = c / λ

Calculation: f = (3 × 10^8) / (15.0 × 10^-6) = 2 × 10^13 Hz

Result: Frequency f = 2 × 10^13 Hz
questions.explanation: Infrared frequency calculation from wavelength.

questions.question: Numerical 2: Frequency of 193 nm UV radiation in laser eye surgery
questions.answer:
Given Data:
Wavelength λ = 193 nm = 193 × 10^-9 mLight speed c = 3 × 10^8 m/s

Formula: f = c / λ

Calculation: f = (3 × 10^8) / (193 × 10^-9) = 1.55 × 10^15 Hz

Result: Frequency f = 1.55 × 10^15 Hz
questions.explanation: High-frequency UV excimer laser radiation.

questions.question: Numerical 3: Wavelength of 100 MHz radio waves in MRI
questions.answer:
Given Data:
Frequency f = 100 MHz = 100 × 10^6 Hz = 10^8 HzSpeed c = 3 × 10^8 m/s

Formula: λ = c / f

Calculation: λ = (3 × 10^8) / (10^8) = 3 m

Result: Wavelength λ = 3 m
questions.explanation: Radio frequency wavelength in medical MRI systems.

questions.question: Numerical 4: Travel time of radio pulse from Sun to Earth
questions.answer:
Given Data:
Distance d = 1.49 × 10^11 mSpeed of light c = 3 × 10^8 m/s

Formula: t = d / c

Calculation: t = (1.49 × 10^11) / (3 × 10^8) = 496.67 s ≈ 8 minutes 16.67 seconds

Result: Travel time = 496.67 s
questions.explanation: Light takes roughly 8.3 minutes to travel from the Sun to Earth.

questions.question: Numerical 5: Distance in kilometers in one light-year
questions.answer:
Given Data:
Speed c = 3 × 10^8 m/s = 3 × 10^5 km/sTime t = 1 year = 365.25 × 24 × 3600 = 3.1536 × 10^7 s

Formula: d = c × t

Calculation: d = (3 × 10^5 km/s) × (3.1536 × 10^7 s) = 9.46 × 10^12 km

Result: 1 Light-Year = 9.46 × 10^12 km (approx 9.33 × 10^12 km depending on STB standard factor 365 days = 3.1536e7 s)
questions.explanation: A light-year is the astronomical distance light travels in one Julian year.

questions.question: Numerical 6: Frequency of green light with wavelength 5.5 × 10^-7 m
questions.answer:
Given Data:
Wavelength λ = 5.5 × 10^-7 mSpeed c = 3 × 10^8 m/s

Formula: f = c / λ

Calculation: f = (3 × 10^8) / (5.5 × 10^-7) = 5.45 × 10^14 Hz

Result: Frequency f = 5.45 × 10^14 Hz
questions.explanation: Visible green spectrum light frequency.

questions.question: Numerical 7: Wavelength of 2.45 GHz microwave oven radiation
questions.answer:
Given Data:
Frequency f = 2.45 GHz = 2.45 × 10^9 HzSpeed c = 3 × 10^8 m/s

Formula: λ = c / f

Calculation: λ = (3 × 10^8) / (2.45 × 10^9) = 0.1224 m = 122.4 mm

Result: Wavelength λ = 0.1224 m (122.4 mm)
questions.explanation: Microwave frequency resonates with water dipole rotation.

questions.question: In a concave mirror, the image size depends upon:

questions.question: a) Define refraction of light. b) Light passage through parallel glass slab. c) Define angle of incidence and angle of refraction. Express laws of refraction.
questions.answer: a) Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one transparent medium into another with different optical density due to a change in speed. b) Light bends toward normal on entering glass and away from normal upon exiting, emerging parallel to incident ray with a lateral shift. c) Laws: 1) Incident ray, refracted ray, and normal lie in the same plane. 2) Snell's Law: sin i / sin r = constant (n).

questions.question: a) What is refractive index? b) How to determine refractive index of glass slab experimentally? c) Which physical quantity remains unaffected when refraction occurs?

questions.question: a) What is a lens? b) Light ray parallel to principal axis entering convex lens? c) Why convex lens is converging? d) Power of lens and units.

questions.question: a) Define critical angle. b) Total internal reflection (TIR). c) Conditions for TIR. d) Practical everyday examples.

questions.question: a) What are optical fibers? b) Describe how TIR is used in an endoscope.

questions.answer: a) Induced emf is proportional to rate of change of magnetic flux (ε = -N dΦ/dt). b) Lenz's Law states induced current flows in a direction opposing the change in flux causing it. Mechanical work done overcoming magnetic opposition converts into electrical energy.
questions.explanation: Electromagnetic induction principles.

questions.question: Explain transformer principle, construction, step-up vs step-down, and role in power transmission.
questions.answer: Principle: Mutual induction between primary and secondary coils on a soft iron core. Formula: Vs / Vp = Ns / Np = Ip / Is. Step-up (Ns > Np) increases voltage for long-distance grid transmission to minimize I²R power loss. Step-down (Ns < Np) lowers voltage safely for homes.
questions.explanation: Transformer power grid physics.

questions.question: Numerical 1: Force on 15 cm wire carrying 4 A current at 30° to 0.8 T field
questions.answer:
Given Data:
I = 4 A, L = 15 cm = 0.15 m, B = 0.8 T, θ = 30°

Formula: F = B I L sin θ

Calculation: F = 0.8 × 4 × 0.15 × sin(30°) = 0.48 × 0.5 = 0.24 N

Result: Force on wire F = 0.24 N
questions.explanation: Magnetic force on current wire.

questions.question: Numerical 2: Torque on 2 cm square loop carrying 2 A current at 30° to 0.7 T field
questions.answer:
Given Data:
Side = 2 cm = 0.02 m => Area A = (0.02)² = 0.0004 m², I = 2 A, B = 0.7 T, α = 30° (plane angle)

Formula: τ = I B A cos α

Calculation: τ = 2 × 0.7 × 0.0004 × cos(30°) = 0.00056 × 0.866 = 4.85 × 10^-4 N·m

Result: Torque τ = 4.8 × 10^-4 N·m
questions.explanation: Magnetic torque on current loop.

questions.question: Numerical 3: Transformer converting 220 V supply to 12 V with 2200 primary turns
questions.answer:
Given Data:
Primary voltage Vp = 220 V, Secondary voltage Vs = 12 V, Primary turns Np = 2200

Formula: Ns / Np = Vs / Vp => Ns = Np × (Vs / Vp)

Calculation: Ns = 2200 × (12 / 220) = 2200 × 0.05454 = 120 turns

Result: Secondary turns Ns = 120 turns
questions.explanation: Step-down transformer turn ratio.

questions.question: Numerical 4: Induced emf in coil surrounding solenoid with mutual induction 5.5 × 10^-5 H and ΔI/Δt = 150 A/s
questions.answer:

Mutual inductance M = 5.5 × 10^-5 HRate of current change ΔI/Δt = 150 A/s

Formula: ε = -M (ΔI / Δt)

Calculation: ε = -(5.5 × 10^-5) × 150 = -8.25 × 10^-3 V (-8.25 mV)

Result: Induced EMF ε = -8.25 × 10^-3 V
questions.explanation: Mutual induction EMF calculation.

questions.question: Cathode rays consist of streams of fast moving:

questions.question: The Boolean expression for a NAND gate is:

questions.question: The electron gun in a Cathode Ray Oscilloscope (CRO) provides:

questions.question: a) Describe construction and working of Cathode Ray Oscilloscope (CRO). b) Uses of CRO.

Fluorescent screen to display light spot. b) Uses: Displaying waveforms, measuring AC/DC voltages, measuring signal frequencies.

questions.question: a) Analogue vs Digital electronics. b) Advantages of digital electronics.
questions.answer: a) Analogue electronics processes continuously variable voltage signals. Digital electronics processes discrete binary signals (0s and 1s). b) Advantages: High noise immunity, easy storage/transmission, high accuracy, compatibility with computers.
questions.explanation: Digital revolution in electronics.

questions.question: Explain basic Logic Gates (AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR) with symbol, truth table, and Boolean expression.
questions.answer: AND: Y = A · B (1 only if both 1). OR: Y = A + B (1 if any 1). NOT: Y = NOT A (inverts). NAND: Y = NOT (A · B). NOR: Y = NOT (A + B).
questions.explanation: Fundamental digital building blocks.

questions.question: In computer terminology, information means:
questions.explanation: Raw data processed into meaningful organized form is information.

questions.question: Which component is the brain of the computer?
questions.explanation: Central Processing Unit executes all instructions and calculations.

questions.question: Which of the following is an input device?
questions.explanation: Keyboards feed user input data into the computer.

questions.question: Optical fiber transmits data in the form of:
questions.explanation: Light pulses bounce internally via Total Internal Reflection.

questions.question: Primary memory of computer includes:
questions.explanation: RAM (volatile) and ROM (non-volatile) form primary storage directly accessible by CPU.

questions.question: a) Define ICT. b) Components of ICT system.
questions.answer: a) ICT refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications (internet, wireless, cellphones). b) Components: Hardware, Software, Data, Procedures, People, Communication Networks.
questions.explanation: Modern communication infrastructure.

questions.question: a) Hardware vs Software. b) Primary vs Secondary memory.
questions.answer: a) Hardware: Physical tangible parts of computer (CPU, monitor, RAM). Software: Set of programs/instructions (OS, applications). b) Primary memory (RAM/ROM) is fast, volatile, directly accessed by CPU. Secondary memory (Hard drive, SSD) is non-volatile long-term storage.
questions.explanation: Computer architecture.

questions.question: Importance of Internet, E-mail, and Cloud Storage in modern society.
questions.answer: Enables instant global communication, information retrieval, remote work, e-commerce, and centralized secure data backup.
questions.explanation: Global connectivity.

questions.question: When an electron jumps from a higher energy orbit E2 to lower energy orbit E1, photon energy emitted is:
questions.explanation: Energy difference is emitted as a single photon.

questions.question: The line spectrum of an element is its:

questions.question: a) Describe Rutherford's α-scattering experiment. b) Postulates and limitations of Rutherford's model.
questions.answer: a) Fired alpha particles at thin gold foil. Most passed straight through, but few deflected at large angles. b) Postulates: Atom has tiny dense positive nucleus with electrons revolving around. Limitations: Classical physics dictates orbiting electrons emit radiation, lose energy, and spiral into nucleus; cannot explain discrete line spectra.

questions.question: a) Postulates of Bohr's Atomic Model. b) Explanation of Hydrogen spectrum.
questions.answer: a) 1. Electrons revolve in non-radiating stable stationary orbits. 2. Angular momentum mvr = nh / 2π. 3. Photon emitted/absorbed when jumping orbits: ΔE = E2 - E1 = h f. b) Transitions down to n=1 (Lyman/UV), n=2 (Balmer/Visible), n=3 (Paschen/IR) form discrete line spectra.

questions.question: The α-radiation is:
questions.explanation: Alpha particles (helium nuclei) carry +2e charge and high mass, yielding intense ionization.

questions.question: A radioactive nuclide emits a β-particle. The atomic number (proton number) of nucleus:
questions.explanation: Beta decay converts a neutron into a proton and electron: Z -> Z + 1.

questions.question: A particle emitted comprising two protons and two neutrons is called:
questions.explanation: Alpha particle is identical to a Helium nucleus (4_2 He).

questions.question: In decay 91Pa233 -> 92U233 + ..., emitted particle is:
questions.explanation: Atomic number increases from 91 to 92 while mass number remains 233, indicating beta decay.

questions.question: The type of radiation that travels in a straight line across an electric field is:
questions.explanation: Gamma rays are neutral EM photons and undergo zero deflection in electric/magnetic fields.

questions.question: A powder contains 100mg radioactive material emitting α-particles. Half-life is 5 days. Mass remaining after 10 days:
questions.explanation: 10 days = 2 half-lives. 100mg -> 50mg (5d) -> 25mg (10d).

questions.question: The main source of energy in the stars is:
questions.explanation: High-temperature fusion of Hydrogen nuclei into Helium powers stars.

questions.question: The splitting of a heavy nucleus into smaller nuclei is called:
questions.explanation: Nuclear fission releases energy and neutrons when heavy nucleus splits.

questions.question: A process in which two light nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus is called:
questions.explanation: Nuclear fusion combines light isotopes like Deuterium and Tritium.

questions.question: Nature and penetrating ability of β-particles:

options.text: Electron / stopped by a few mm of aluminum

questions.optionsRaw: c) Electron / stopped by a few mm of aluminum
questions.correctAnswer: c) Electron / stopped by a few mm of aluminum
questions.explanation: Beta particles are high-speed electrons stopped by a few millimeters of aluminum sheet.

questions.question: a) Define radioactivity. b) Stable vs Unstable nucleus. c) Why some elements are radioactive?
questions.answer: a) Radioactivity is the spontaneous, uncontrollable disintegration of unstable atomic nuclei accompanied by emission of radiation (α, β, γ). b) Stable nuclei have balanced neutron-to-proton ratio (N/Z ~ 1 to 1.5) and do not decay. c) Unstable heavy elements (Z > 82) have excess nuclear repulsion forces, decaying spontaneously to reach stability.
questions.explanation: Nuclear decay fundamentals.

questions.question: Uranium decay 92U238 -> 90Th234 + 2He4. State proton and nucleon numbers of alpha and thorium.
questions.answer: Alpha particle: Proton number = 2, Nucleon number = 4. Thorium nuclide: Proton number = 90, Nucleon number = 234.
questions.explanation: Alpha decay conservation of mass/charge.

questions.question: a) Random nature of radioactive decay. b) Gamma ray safety measures.
questions.answer: a) Radioactive decay is a purely stochastic quantum process; impossible to predict exactly when a specific nucleus will decay, though decay rate follows half-life statistics. b) Safety: Lead shielding, maximum distance, minimal exposure time.
questions.explanation: Radioactive statistics and safety.

questions.question: a) Define half-life (T1/2) of radioactive element. b) Half-life formula.
questions.answer: a) Half-life is the time required for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay. b) N(t) = N0 (1/2)^(t / T1/2) or T1/2 = 0.693 / λ.
questions.explanation: Nuclear half-life law.

questions.question: Fission vs Fusion comparison. Applications.
questions.answer: Fission: Splitting heavy nucleus (e.g. U-235) into lighter fragments by slow neutrons; used in Nuclear Power Plants. Fusion: Combining light nuclei (e.g. Hydrogen) at ultra-high temperatures; powers the Sun and hydrogen bombs.
questions.explanation: Nuclear energy processes.

questions.question: Numerical 1: C-14 decay in 12,900-year-old wood sample (Half-life = 5730 yr, Initial = 15.3 dpm/g)
questions.answer:
Given Data:
Initial activity A0 = 15.3 dpm/gTime t = 12,900 yrHalf-life T1/2 = 5730 yr

Formula: Half-lives n = t / T1/2 = 12900 / 5730 = 2.2513Activity A = A0 (1/2)^n

Calculation: A = 15.3 × (0.5)^2.2513 = 15.3 × 0.2099 = 3.21 dpm/g (2.2513 half lives, ~0.21 remaining fraction, 3.2 dpm/g)

Result: Remaining C-14 activity = 3.21 dpm/g
questions.explanation: Radiocarbon dating calculation.

questions.question: Numerical 2: Maximum measurable age for C-14 activity threshold 0.20%
questions.answer:
Given Data:
Remaining fraction A / A0 = 0.20% = 0.0020Half-life T1/2 = 5730 yr

Formula: (1/2)^n = 0.0020 => n log(0.5) = log(0.0020) => n = -2.6989 / -0.3010 = 8.9657Age t = n × T1/2 = 8.9657 × 5730 = 51,374 years

Calculation: Maximum age limit = 51,374 years

Result: Carbon dating operational threshold limit.

questions.question: Numerical 3: Time required for 25% of C-14 atoms in sample to decay
questions.answer:
Given Data:
Decayed fraction = 25% => Remaining fraction A / A0 = 75% = 0.75Half-life T1/2 = 5730 yr

Formula: (1/2)^n = 0.75 => n = log(0.75) / log(0.5) = -0.1249 / -0.3010 = 0.4150Time t = 0.4150 × 5730 = 2378 years

Calculation: Time to decay 25% = 2378 years

Result: Partial radioactive decay duration.

questions.question: Numerical 4: Age of excavated wood sample with decay rate 0.109 dps/g vs modern tree 0.296 dps/g
questions.answer:
Given Data:
Initial activity A0 = 0.296 dps/gPresent activity A = 0.109 dps/gHalf-life T1/2 = 5730 yr

Formula: A / A0 = 0.109 / 0.296 = 0.3682(1/2)^n = 0.3682 => n = log(0.3682) / log(0.5) = -0.4339 / -0.3010 = 1.4414Age t = 1.4414 × 5730 = 8258 years

Calculation: Age of archaeological object = 8258 years

Result: Archaeological radiocarbon dating result.

questions.question: A girl throws a small stone into a lake. Waves spread out from where the stone hits the water and travel to the bank of the lake. She notices that ten waves reach the side of the pond in a time of 5.0 s. What is the frequency of the waves?
questions.explanation: Frequency is defined as the number of complete waves passing a point per second. Using f = N / t = 10 / 5.0 s = 2.0 Hz.

questions.question: Water waves can be used to show reflection, refraction, and diffraction. For each of these, which row shows whether or not the speed of the water waves changes?

options.text: Reflection: No / Refraction: Yes / Diffraction: No

questions.optionsRaw: c) Reflection: No / Refraction: Yes / Diffraction: No
questions.correctAnswer: c) Reflection: No / Refraction: Yes / Diffraction: No
questions.explanation: During reflection and diffraction, the wave remains in the same medium, so its speed remains constant. In refraction, the wave moves from one medium/depth to another, which changes its speed.

questions.question: The diagrams show water waves that move more slowly after passing into shallow water. Which diagram shows what happens to the waves?
questions.explanation: When water waves pass into shallow water, their speed and wavelength decrease, causing wavefronts to get closer together and bend toward the normal.

questions.question: The diagram shows a water wave approaching a barrier with a gap. The wave reaches point P. What is the name of the effect that causes the wave to reach point P?
questions.explanation: Diffraction is the spreading of waves as they pass through an aperture or around an obstacle into the shadow region.

questions.question: Water waves pass from deep into the shallow region then refracted. The characteristic of wave which will remain constant is:
questions.explanation: The frequency of a wave is determined solely by the source generating the wave and remains unchanged during refraction.

questions.question: Which is not a characteristic of wave?
questions.explanation: Waves transfer energy and momentum without transporting mass. Wavelength, amplitude, period, and velocity are wave characteristics.

questions.question: How spherical wavefronts are produced in the ripple tank?
questions.answer: Spherical wavefronts are produced by using a point dipper (a small spherical ball attached to the vibrator) that touches the water surface at a single point.
questions.explanation: As the point dipper oscillates vertically, it creates circular/spherical ripples that expand uniformly outward in all directions.

questions.question: What is the difference between displacement and amplitude of the wave?
questions.answer: Displacement (x) is the distance of a vibrating particle from its equilibrium position at any given instant. Amplitude (A) is the maximum displacement of a particle from its equilibrium position.
questions.explanation: Displacement varies continuously from zero to maximum, whereas amplitude is a fixed constant representing peak displacement.

questions.question: Derive the relation between wave speed and frequency.
questions.answer: v = f λ
questions.explanation: Speed is distance divided by time (v = S / t). For one full wave cycle, distance S = λ (wavelength) and time t = T (period). Thus v = λ / T. Since frequency f = 1 / T, substituting gives v = f λ.

questions.question: When an oscillating object is in simple harmonic motion, its maximum speed occurs when the object is at its:
questions.explanation: At the equilibrium point, all potential energy is converted into kinetic energy, so speed is maximum.

questions.question: In an oscillating pendulum, the bob accelerates from its extreme position due to:
questions.explanation: The restoring component of gravity (mg sin θ) pulls the bob back toward the central rest position.

questions.question: In the ball and bowl system, the mean position is at:
questions.explanation: At the center of the bowl, net force acting on the ball is zero (normal reaction balances weight).

questions.question: Oscillations are damped due to the presence of:
questions.explanation: Damping occurs when resistive/frictional forces dissipate mechanical energy into thermal energy.

questions.question: Define the term transverse wave.
questions.answer: A transverse wave is a wave in which the particles of the medium vibrate perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation.
questions.explanation: Examples include water waves, light waves, and waves on a plucked string.

questions.question: Define the term longitudinal wave.
questions.answer: A longitudinal wave is a wave in which the particles of the medium vibrate parallel to the direction of wave propagation.
questions.explanation: It consists of compressions (high density) and rarefactions (low density). Examples include sound waves and slinky compression waves.

questions.question: a) Write a short note on the mechanical wave. b) How can you say that mechanical waves are also material waves?
questions.answer: a) Mechanical waves require a physical material medium (solid, liquid, or gas) to travel and transmit energy. b) They are called material waves because energy transfer depends entirely on elastic collisions between material particles of the medium.
questions.explanation: They cannot propagate through a vacuum (e.g. sound waves, water waves).

questions.question: Waves are the means of energy transfer without matter. Justify this statement with the help of everyday life examples.
questions.answer: When a stone is dropped into a pond, water ripples move outward and cause a distant floating leaf to bob up and down at its position without traveling along with the wave to the shore.
questions.explanation: This proves that energy is transferred across distances while the medium particles only oscillate locally about their mean position.

questions.question: a) Define amplitude, period, frequency, and wavelength. b) Derive v = f λ.
questions.answer: a) Amplitude: Maximum displacement from equilibrium position. Period (T): Time taken for one complete oscillation. Frequency (f): Number of complete cycles per second. Wavelength (λ): Distance between two consecutive crests/compressions. b) Derived from v = S/t = λ/T = f λ.
questions.explanation: Key fundamental wave relationships.

questions.question: a) What is a ripple tank, and explain its working? b) Define wavefront.
questions.answer: a) A ripple tank is a shallow glass tray filled with water, illuminated from above, used to demonstrate wave reflection, refraction, and diffraction. Motorized dippers generate periodic water waves whose crests/troughs appear as light/dark bands on a screen underneath. b) A wavefront is a surface or line joining all points vibrating in the same phase.
questions.explanation: Essential laboratory tool for wave optics and dynamics.

questions.question: Reference an experiment to explain the refraction of waves concerning the ripple tank.
questions.answer: Place a flat glass plate in part of the ripple tank to decrease water depth. When water waves pass from deep water to shallow water at an angle, their speed and wavelength decrease, causing the wavefronts to bend toward the normal line.
questions.explanation: Demonstrates refraction due to medium density/depth change.

questions.question: What is the phenomenon of diffraction?
questions.answer: Diffraction is the bending or spreading of wave wavefronts around the corners of obstacles or through narrow gaps/apertures into the shadow region.
questions.explanation: Diffraction is most pronounced when the gap size is comparable to the wavelength.

questions.question: a) What is simple harmonic motion (SHM)? b) What are the necessary conditions for a body to execute SHM?
questions.answer: a) SHM is periodic motion where acceleration is directly proportional to displacement from the mean position and directed toward the mean position (a ∝ -x). b) Conditions: 1. Restoring force proportional to displacement (F = -kx). 2. System possesses inertia and elasticity. 3. Minimal friction/damping.
questions.explanation: Governs linear restoring systems.

questions.question: a) Explain SHM in a simple pendulum. b) Effect on period if: i) length increases, ii) mass increases.
questions.answer: a) A pendulum bob displaced by angle θ experiences a restoring gravitational force component (mg sin θ) pulling it toward the mean position. b) i) Increasing length L increases time period T (since T ∝ √L). ii) Mass has no effect on period T.
questions.explanation: Formula: T = 2π √(L/g).

questions.question: a) Explain SHM in the ball and bowl system. b) Why is ball speed maximum at equilibrium position?
questions.answer: a) When a ball is released from an elevated rim point A in a smooth bowl, gravity pulls it toward the central mean position O. Momentum carries it to opposite point B, oscillating in SHM. b) At equilibrium, all potential energy is converted into kinetic energy (PE=0, KE=max).
questions.explanation: Demonstrates gravitational restoring motion.

questions.question: a) What are damped oscillations? b) How does damping reduce amplitude? c) Why does a swing's amplitude decrease with time?
questions.answer: a) Damped oscillations are vibrations whose amplitude decreases progressively over time due to resistive forces. b) Friction and air resistance perform negative work, dissipating energy into heat. c) Air drag and hinge friction drain energy from the swing until it stops.
questions.explanation: Energy dissipation in real physical systems.

questions.question: Sound is a form of:
questions.explanation: Sound requires a material medium to propagate and transfers mechanical energy through particle vibrations.

questions.question: Audible frequencies range that a normal human ear can detect is:
questions.explanation: The human audible frequency spectrum spans from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz).

questions.question: The approximate value of the speed of sound in air at 0°C temperature is:
questions.explanation: At standard temperature and pressure (0°C), the speed of sound in dry air is 331 m/s.

questions.question: Sound travels faster in solids as compared to gases because of:
questions.optionsRaw: c) Solid molecules are packed tightly.
questions.correctAnswer: c) Solid molecules are packed tightly.
questions.explanation: Tight molecular packing in solids results in higher elasticity and quicker particle-to-particle energy transmission.

questions.question: The two factors that affect the speed of sound in air are:

options.text: Temperature and humidity of the air

questions.optionsRaw: d) Temperature and humidity of the air
questions.correctAnswer: d) Temperature and humidity of the air
questions.explanation: Increasing air temperature and humidity both reduce density, thereby increasing sound speed.

questions.question: The separation between two consecutive compressions of the sound wave is called:
questions.explanation: Wavelength in a longitudinal wave is the distance between consecutive compressions or rarefactions.

questions.question: The order of speed of the sound in different mediums from faster to slowest is:
questions.explanation: Sound travels fastest in dense solids (e.g. steel ~5960 m/s), slower in liquids (~1498 m/s in water), slowest in gases (~340 m/s in air).

questions.question: Ultrasound has several uses in medicine and industry. Which one has use of ultrasound?
questions.explanation: High-frequency ultrasound waves (2-18 MHz) are non-invasive and safe for fetal imaging.

questions.question: The cause of the echo is:
questions.explanation: An echo is caused by the reflection of sound waves off a hard surface back to the listener.

questions.question: Which type of wave cannot travel through a vacuum?
questions.explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave requiring physical particle vibrations and cannot propagate in a vacuum.

questions.question: a) How is sound produced? b) Describe compressions and rarefactions with a diagram.
questions.answer: a) Sound is produced by vibrating bodies that disturb adjacent air particles. b) Compressions are high-pressure, high-density regions where particles are pushed together. Rarefactions are low-pressure, low-density regions where particles spread apart.

questions.question: a) Why are sound waves referred to as mechanical waves? b) Cite an experiment proving sound requires a medium.
questions.answer: a) Sound waves require a physical material medium (solid, liquid, or gas) to transmit vibrations. b) Bell Jar Experiment: Place an electric bell inside an airtight glass jar connected to a vacuum pump. As air is evacuated, the ringing sound fades until it becomes silent, proving sound cannot travel in a vacuum.

questions.question: a) Distinguish between musical sound and noise. b) How is noise harmful to humans?
questions.answer: a) Musical sound consists of regular, periodic, pleasing vibrations. Noise consists of irregular, non-periodic, unpleasant vibrations. b) Prolonged noise exposure causes stress, hearing loss, hypertension, and sleep disruption.
questions.explanation: Acoustic quality and noise pollution impacts.

questions.question: a) Define quality or timbre of sound. b) Can two waves from different instruments combine into one wave?
questions.answer: a) Quality or timbre is the characteristic of sound that enables us to distinguish between two notes of the same pitch and loudness produced by different instruments due to different waveforms/overtones. b) Yes, superposing waves construct a resultant complex wave.
questions.explanation: Overtones determine sound texture.

questions.question: a) Why is sound speed greater in solids than liquids/gases? b) Effect of temperature and humidity on sound speed in air.
questions.answer: a) Solids have much higher elastic moduli (stiffness) and tightly packed molecules, transmitting disturbance forces rapidly. b) i) Increasing temperature increases air particle kinetic energy, raising sound speed (~0.6 m/s per °C). ii) Increasing humidity replaces heavier N2/O2 molecules with lighter H2O molecules, reducing air density and increasing sound speed.
questions.explanation: Dependence of acoustic velocity on medium elasticity and density.

questions.question: a) Define echo. b) Explain working and applications of SONAR. c) Detection of defects in metal blocks using ultrasound.
questions.answer: a) An echo is the repetition of sound caused by the reflection of sound waves from a distant hard barrier. b) SONAR (Sound Navigation and Ranging) transmits ultrasonic pulses downward into water and measures the return echo time to determine seabed depth or underwater objects (d = v · t / 2). c) Ultrasonic waves sent through metal blocks pass through clean metal but reflect back early from internal cracks/flaws.
questions.explanation: Acoustic reflection diagnostic applications.

questions.question: a) Define Infrasonic, Audible range, Ultrasound. b) How is ultrasound used for cleaning? c) Two medical imaging uses of ultrasound.
questions.answer: a) Infrasonic: Sound below 20 Hz. Audible range: 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Ultrasound: Sound above 20,000 Hz (20 kHz). b) High-frequency ultrasonic vibrations in cleaning solutions dislodge dirt from intricate instrument parts. c) i) Pre-natal fetal monitoring. ii) Echocardiography for heart imaging.
questions.explanation: Frequency classification and medical/industrial ultrasound.

questions.question: Product of resistance and capacitance equal to?

questions.explanation: Dimensionally: R = V / I = J / (C · A), C = Q / V = C / V. R · C = (V / I) · (Q / V) = Q / I = (A · s) / A = Seconds.

questions.question: Numerical 1: Speed of sound in air at 50°C
questions.answer:

Formula: vt = 331 + 0.6 × T

Calculation: vt = 331 + 0.6 × 50 = 331 + 30 = 361.0 m/s

Result: Speed of sound at 50°C = 361.0 m/s

questions.question: Numerical 2: Wavelengths corresponding to human audible frequency range

questions.explanation: Higher frequency corresponds to shorter wavelength.

questions.question: Numerical 3: Submarine depth measurement using ultrasonic pulse
questions.answer:
Given Data:
Echo time t = 40 ms = 0.040 sSound speed in seawater v = 1480 m/s

Formula: d = (v × t) / 2

Calculation: d = (1480 × 0.040) / 2 = 59.2 / 2 = 29.6 m ≈ 30 m

Result: Submarine depth = 29.6 m (rounded to 30 m)
questions.explanation: Echo travels down to sea-bed and back, so single-way depth is half the total distance.

questions.question: Numerical 4: Bat echolocation prey detection
questions.answer:
Given Data:
Wavelength λ = 0.0080 m, Speed in air v = 340 m/s, Return echo time t = 0.10 s

Formula: i) f = v / λii) Total distance = v × tiii) Prey distance d = (v × t) / 2

Calculation: i) f = 340 / 0.0080 = 42,500 Hz = 42.5 kHzii) Total pulse distance = 340 × 0.10 = 34 miii) Prey distance = 34 / 2 = 17 m

Result: i) Frequency = 42.5 kHzii) Total pulse distance = 34 miii) Distance to prey = 17 m
questions.explanation: Bat echolocation uses ultrasonic reflection to pinpoint prey distance.

questions.question: The optical phenomenon in which the splitting of white light into seven distinct colors occurs is called:
questions.explanation: Dispersion is the separation of composite white light into constituent spectrum colors due to wavelength-dependent refraction.

questions.question: a) Define dispersion of light. b) Describe dispersion when white light passes through a glass prism.
questions.answer: a) Dispersion is the splitting of composite white light into its constituent spectral colors when passing through a refracting medium. b) When white light enters a glass prism, each constituent wavelength refracts at a slightly different angle because glass refractive index varies with wavelength. Red (longest λ) bends least, while Violet (shortest λ) bends most, producing a VIBGYOR spectrum.
questions.explanation: Prism refracts colors according to wavelength.

questions.question: a) Explain how a rainbow is produced on a rainy day. b) How are spectrum colors related to frequency/wavelength?
questions.answer: a) Millions of airborne raindrops act as tiny glass prisms. Sunlight entering a raindrop refracts, internally reflects off the back wall, and refracts again upon exiting, dispersing light into a rainbow arc. b) Violet has the highest frequency and shortest wavelength (~400 nm); Red has the lowest frequency and longest wavelength (~700 nm).
questions.explanation: Atmospheric dispersion and internal reflection.

questions.question: a) What are electromagnetic waves? b) List main EM components in decreasing order of wavelength. c) Do UV rays travel faster than radio waves in a vacuum?
questions.answer: a) EM waves are transverse non-mechanical waves consisting of oscillating electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to each other and to propagation direction. b) Decreasing wavelength: Radio waves > Microwaves > Infrared > Visible Light > Ultraviolet > X-rays > Gamma rays. c) No, all EM waves travel at the exact same speed in a vacuum (c = 3 × 10^8 m/s).
questions.explanation: Maxwellian electromagnetic wave principles.

questions.question: Compare properties of UV rays and radio signals: a) Faster speed in vacuum? b) Greater frequency? c) Greater wavelength?
questions.answer: a) Both have equal speed in a vacuum (c = 3 × 10^8 m/s). b) Ultraviolet rays have a much greater frequency than radio waves. c) Radio waves have a much greater wavelength than UV rays.
questions.explanation: Speed is constant c = f λ.

questions.question: a) What are main sources of radio waves? b) Main advantage of radio waves in communication?
questions.answer: a) Radio transmitters (oscillating LC circuits/antennas), astronomical objects (stars, pulsars). b) Long wavelength allows radio waves to diffract around buildings, pass through atmospheric obstacles, and travel vast distances.
questions.explanation: Telecommunication foundations.

questions.question: Why are microwaves preferred in satellite communication?
questions.answer: Microwaves (high frequency, short wavelength) can pass straight through the Earth's ionosphere without reflection or significant absorption, establishing direct line-of-sight links with orbiting satellites.
questions.explanation: Ionospheric transmission window.

questions.question: a) Radiation used in TV remote controllers? b) How do molecules emit infrared? c) How do intruder alarms visualize thermal images?
questions.answer: a) Infrared radiation. b) Thermal vibrations and rotations of charged molecular bonds emit infrared photons. c) Passive Infrared (PIR) sensors detect changes in thermal IR patterns emitted by moving human body heat against cool surroundings.
questions.explanation: Infrared technology applications.

questions.question: a) Principle of optical fibers? b) Daily life applications in telecommunications and medical industry.
questions.answer: a) Total Internal Reflection (TIR) inside a high-refractive-index core surrounded by lower-index cladding. b) i) Telecommunications: High-speed fiber optic internet transmitting data pulses at light speed over long distances without electrical loss. ii) Medical: Endoscopes for non-surgical internal organ imaging.
questions.explanation: Fiber optics and total internal reflection.

questions.question: a) Sunlight exposure and skin damage. b) Why UV rays are used under medical supervision in sunbeds.
questions.answer: a) Sunlight contains UV-A and UV-B radiation that can damage cellular DNA and cause sunburn or skin cancer. Controlled short exposure stimulates Vitamin D synthesis. b) Controlled UV dosages treat skin disorders like psoriasis while avoiding carcinogenic tissue damage.
questions.explanation: Biological impacts of ultraviolet radiation.

questions.question: a) Explain fluorescence. b) Describe sterilization using UV light.
questions.answer: a) Fluorescence is the absorption of higher-frequency UV radiation by a material, which re-emits visible light photons almost instantaneously. b) Short-wavelength UV-C radiation destroys bacterial and viral DNA/RNA, sterilizing medical instruments and water.
questions.explanation: Photonic absorption and sterilization.

questions.question: X-rays are used to detect cracks in metals. Explain how.
questions.answer: High-energy X-rays penetrate dense metal components and strike a photographic film or digital detector behind them. Cracks or internal voids allow more X-rays through, creating dark lines on the radiograph.
questions.explanation: Industrial radiography inspection.

questions.question: a) Origin of gamma rays? b) Radiosurgery cancer treatment. c) Hospital medical imaging applications.
questions.answer: a) Gamma rays originate from de-excitation transitions within unstable radioactive atomic nuclei. b) Gamma Knife radiosurgery focuses multiple weak gamma beams from different angles onto a deep brain tumor to destroy cancer cells without harming healthy tissue. c) PET scans and SPECT imaging use gamma-emitting tracers for diagnostic body scans.
questions.explanation: Nuclear medical radiation applications.

questions.explanation: High-frequency UV excimer laser radiation.

questions.question: a) Define reflection of light. b) Diagram on plane surface. c) Define Normal, Angle of Incidence, Angle of Reflection. d) Express laws of reflection.
questions.answer: a) Reflection is the bouncing back of light rays when they strike a polished surface. b) Plane mirror setup showing incident ray, normal, and reflected ray. c) i) Normal: Perpendicular line drawn to surface at point of incidence. ii) Angle of Incidence (i): Angle between incident ray and normal. iii) Angle of Reflection (r): Angle between reflected ray and normal. d) Laws: 1) θi = θr. 2) Incident ray, reflected ray, and normal lie in the same plane.
questions.explanation: Fundamental law of optics.

questions.question: Name the type of mirror used in: a) Side / rear view mirror. b) Blind spots on hilly roads. c) Dentist mirror.
questions.answer: a) Convex mirror (provides erect, diminished wide field of view). b) Convex mirror (gives wide angled view around blind curves). c) Concave mirror (produces magnified upright image when close).
questions.explanation: Practical mirror applications.

questions.question: a) Define refraction of light. b) Light passage through parallel glass slab. c) Define angle of incidence and angle of refraction. Express laws of refraction.
questions.answer: a) Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one transparent medium into another with different optical density due to a change in speed. b) Light bends toward normal on entering glass and away from normal upon exiting, emerging parallel to incident ray with a lateral shift. c) Laws: 1) Incident ray, refracted ray, and normal lie in the same plane. 2) Snell's Law: sin i / sin r = constant (n).
questions.explanation: Snell's Law and refraction mechanics.

questions.question: a) What is refractive index? b) How to determine refractive index of glass slab experimentally? c) Which physical quantity remains unaffected when refraction occurs?
questions.answer: a) Refractive index n = c / v (ratio of light speed in vacuum to speed in medium). b) Trace incident and refracted ray through glass slab using pins, measure angles i and r, calculate n = sin i / sin r. c) Frequency of light remains completely unaffected.
questions.explanation: Refractive index properties.

questions.question: a) What is a glass prism? b) Passage of monochromatic light through prism. c) Ray entering prism surface at: i) 0° with normal, ii) 30° with normal.
questions.answer: a) A glass prism is a transparent solid with two triangular ends and three rectangular sides. b) Light refracts twice (at entry and exit faces), deviating toward the base by deviation angle D. c) i) At 0° (along normal), light enters without changing direction; speed and wavelength decrease, frequency stays constant. ii) At 30°, light bends toward normal inside glass; frequency stays constant, speed, wavelength, and direction change.
questions.explanation: Prismatic refraction principles.

questions.question: a) What is a lens? b) Light ray parallel to principal axis entering convex lens? c) Why convex lens is converging? d) Power of lens and units.
questions.answer: a) A lens is a piece of transparent glass bounded by two spherical surfaces. b) Rays parallel to principal axis refract through the focal point F. c) Convex lens bends incoming parallel rays inward toward the central axis, converging them at a real focus point. d) Power P = 1 / f (in meters). SI unit is Diopter (D).
questions.explanation: Lens focal geometry.

questions.question: a) Define critical angle. b) Total internal reflection (TIR). c) Conditions for TIR. d) Practical everyday examples.
questions.answer: a) Critical angle (θc) is the angle of incidence in a denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the rarer medium is 90°. b) When angle of incidence in denser medium exceeds θc, light is 100% reflected back into the denser medium. c) Conditions: 1. Light travels from denser to rarer medium. 2. Angle of incidence > θc. d) Examples: Sparkle of diamond, mirage in deserts, fiber optic cables.
questions.explanation: TIR physics and applications.

questions.question: Determine critical angle of light in diamond (refractive index n = 2.41).
questions.explanation: Diamond's small critical angle causes intense internal light trapping and brilliant sparkling.

questions.question: a) What are optical fibers? b) Describe how TIR is used in an endoscope.
questions.answer: a) Optical fibers are ultra-thin flexible glass/plastic strands consisting of a high-index core and lower-index cladding that guide light via TIR. b) An endoscope uses a bundle of optical fibers to carry illumination into the stomach/organs and return high-resolution images to a monitor.
questions.explanation: Medical endoscopy and fiber optic guidance.

questions.question: a) Ray diagram of magnifying glass. b) Using thin converging lens as magnifying glass. c) Magnification formula.
questions.answer: a) Object placed between optical center O and principal focus F creates a magnified, erect, virtual image on the same side. b) Holds object within focal length (p < f). c) Magnification M = 1 + (D / f), where D = 25 cm (least distance of distinct vision).
questions.explanation: Simple magnifier optical setup.

questions.question: Give magnifying powers of: i) Simple microscope, ii) Compound microscope, iii) Refracting telescope.
questions.answer: i) Simple microscope: M = 1 + (D / f). ii) Compound microscope: M = (L / fo) × (1 + D / fe). iii) Refracting telescope: M = fo / fe.
questions.explanation: Standard optical instrument magnification equations.

questions.question: a) Short-sight vs Long-sight. b) How corrected? c) Why normal eye cannot see objects closer than 25 cm?
questions.answer: a) Short-sight (Myopia): Can see nearby objects clearly but distant objects are blurry. Long-sight (Hypermetropia): Can see distant objects clearly but nearby objects are blurry. b) Myopia is corrected by concave lens; Hypermetropia is corrected by convex lens. c) The ciliary eye muscles cannot squeeze the lens beyond its maximum convexity limit to focus closer than 25 cm (near point).
questions.explanation: Vision defects and eye accommodation limits.

questions.question: Why narrow beam of white light is used in the experiment?
questions.answer: A narrow beam minimizes spherical aberration and overlapping spectral bands, yielding sharp, clear spectrum lines.
questions.explanation: Narrow light slits prevent blurred overlapping color bands.

questions.question: List everyday examples of reflection of light.
questions.answer: Seeing your face in a bathroom mirror, viewing reflections of trees in calm lake water, and rear-view vehicle mirrors.
questions.explanation: Regular specular reflection from smooth polished surfaces.

questions.question: Why angle of incidence is always equal to angle of reflection?
questions.answer: Because light rays obey Fermat's principle of least time and wave phase boundary continuity at smooth reflecting surfaces.
questions.explanation: Law of reflection: θi = θr.

questions.question: Why near-sightedness (myopia) makes far-away objects look blurry?
questions.answer: Because the eyeball is too long or lens too strong, focusing rays from distant objects in front of the retina instead of on it.
questions.explanation: Myopia optical focus defect.

questions.question: What is the most common treatment for refractive error of long-sight?
questions.answer: Wearing convex (converging) corrective eyeglasses or contact lenses.
questions.explanation: Convex lenses provide additional converging power to bring image focus forward onto the retina.
